body:
Energy and economic activity

Energy is essential for producing goods, transporting people, operating machinery, irrigating fields and meeting household needs. India obtains energy from several sources because no single fuel is equally suitable for every purpose. Coal is important for electricity generation and industry, petroleum products dominate many transport applications, and natural gas is used in cooking, industry, fertiliser production and electricity generation.

An energy system includes the resources from which energy is obtained, the processes that convert those resources into usable forms, the infrastructure that transports them and the activities that consume them. Understanding these stages is necessary for interpreting India's energy mix and identifying its energy-security challenges.

Primary and secondary energy

Primary energy is energy available from a natural source before conversion into another energy carrier. Secondary energy is obtained by transforming primary energy into a more convenient form for use or transportation.

Coal, crude oil, natural gas, sunlight and flowing water are primary energy sources. Electricity generated from coal, natural gas, flowing water or sunlight is a secondary energy carrier. Petrol and diesel are also secondary energy products because crude petroleum must first be refined.

Primary sourceConversion or processingUseful output
CoalCombustion in a thermal power stationElectricity
Crude petroleumRefiningPetrol, diesel, LPG and other products
Natural gasProcessing and distributionPipeline gas, CNG and industrial fuel
SunlightSolar photovoltaic conversionElectricity
Flowing waterHydroelectric generationElectricity

The distinction matters because the fuel used to generate electricity and the electricity delivered to consumers represent different stages of the same energy flow. Adding them without accounting for conversion would count some energy twice.

Renewable and non-renewable sources

Renewable energy sources are replenished naturally on timescales relevant to human use. Examples include solar, wind and flowing water. Non-renewable sources, such as coal, petroleum and natural gas, form over geological periods and cannot be replenished at the rate at which people consume them.

Renewable does not mean that an energy source operates continuously. Solar generation varies with sunlight, while wind generation depends on wind conditions. Conversely, non-renewable does not mean that a source cannot provide reliable electricity; a coal-fired plant can generate power when fuel and operating conditions permit, but it consumes a finite resource.

Conventional and non-conventional energy

The expressions conventional and non-conventional describe historical patterns of use rather than whether a resource can be renewed. Traditional textbooks place coal, petroleum, natural gas, firewood and large hydropower among conventional sources. Solar, wind, tidal and geothermal energy are commonly described as non-conventional sources.

These classifications are not interchangeable. Firewood is traditionally used and may be renewable when harvested sustainably. Coal is conventional and non-renewable. Solar energy is commonly classified as non-conventional and renewable. Nuclear energy uses an exhaustible mineral fuel and is not a fossil-fuel energy source.

Commercial energy and final consumption

Commercial energy is bought and sold, such as electricity, coal, petrol and piped gas. Traditional non-commercial energy includes locally collected firewood, crop residues and dung used without a formal market transaction. The same physical material may become commercial energy when it is sold.

Final energy consumption measures energy delivered for use by sectors such as industry, transport and households, after the main energy-conversion processes. A factory purchasing electricity is a final consumer of electricity, while a power station burning coal to produce that electricity is performing an energy transformation.

Prelims focus

  • Coal, crude oil and natural gas are primary fossil energy sources.
  • Electricity is a secondary energy carrier, regardless of whether it comes from coal, water or sunlight.
  • Petrol and diesel are products obtained by refining crude petroleum.
  • Renewable and conventional are different classifications.
  • Trap: Electricity generated from coal is not a separate natural primary energy source.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter Sources of Energy; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 30–34; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 8, Infrastructure, section 8.5, Energy.]

title: India's Energy System: Sources, Conversion and Uses

body:
What an energy mix measures

An energy mix is the combination of sources used to meet energy needs. It must always be interpreted with reference to what is being measured. India's total primary energy supply, final energy consumption and electricity generation have different fuel compositions because they describe different stages of the energy system.

For example, crude oil is important in primary energy supply because petroleum products are widely consumed in transport. Coal is particularly prominent in electricity generation. A household may consume electricity produced from coal without directly purchasing coal.

Total primary energy supply

Total Primary Energy Supply (TPES) measures energy available to the economy from primary sources, using an energy-balance accounting framework. It considers domestic energy production and relevant international trade and stock changes. It is not the same as electricity generated or energy finally consumed.

According to Energy Statistics India 2026, India's TPES was 932,816 thousand tonnes of oil equivalent (ktoe) in financial year 2024–25. This was an increase of 2.95% over 2023–24. The reported figures for 2024–25 are provisional.

The major shares of primary supply in that report were 59.21% for coal including lignite, 29.79% for crude oil and 7.12% for natural gas. Thus, coal was the dominant primary energy source in the reported accounting framework.

For comparison, the same publication reported coal at 57.41%, crude oil at 36.29% and natural gas at 7.31% in 2015–16. These figures show that coal remained dominant while the reported crude-oil share declined over the period. A decline in percentage share does not necessarily mean that the absolute quantity consumed declined.

India's final energy consumption

Total final energy consumption was 608,578 ktoe in 2024–25, according to the same provisional publication. Final consumption includes energy used in sectors such as industry, transport and households rather than fuel consumed to generate electricity.

Energy carrier or fuelShare of final energy consumption, 2024–25
Oil products39.83%
Coal, including lignite28.66%
Electricity22.93%
Natural gas8.58%

The largest entry in this final-consumption table is oil products, not coal. This does not contradict coal's leading position in primary energy supply: coal used in power stations is transformed into electricity, whereas refined petroleum products are delivered directly to many final users.

Do not subtract final consumption from primary supply and treat the difference as electricity-generation losses. Energy balances also contain transformation inputs, conversion losses, energy-sector use and other accounting adjustments. The two totals describe different stages and must be compared through the complete energy balance.

Electricity generation is a third measure

The same publication reported the following shares of electricity actually generated in 2024–25: thermal generation 77.01%, hydropower 7.24%, nuclear power 2.75% and renewable sources other than hydropower 13.00%. Here, thermal generation includes fossil-fuel-based thermal stations; it must not automatically be interpreted as coal alone.

These are shares of electricity generation, not installed generating capacity. A large installed solar or wind capacity does not guarantee an identical share of electricity output because actual generation depends on sunlight, wind, maintenance and operating hours.

How to interpret energy data correctly

TermWhat it measuresCommon unit
Installed capacityRated power-producing capabilityMW or GW
Electricity generationElectrical energy produced over a periodkWh, MU or BU
Fuel productionPhysical amount of fuel extractedTonnes or cubic metres
Energy supply or consumptionEnergy quantity after conversion to common energy unitsMJ, PJ or ktoe

1 GW equals 1,000 MW. One million units (MU) of electricity equals 1 million kWh, while 1 billion units (BU) equals 1 billion kWh. A plant rated at 100 MW does not necessarily generate 100 MW throughout the year; its annual electricity production depends on how long and how heavily it operates.

The latest figures used on this page are from Energy Statistics India 2026, released on 30 March 2026, using 2024–25 provisional data. They describe a specified data period and are not estimates for November 2026.

Prelims focus

  • In 2024–25 provisional data, coal including lignite accounted for 59.21% of reported TPES.
  • Oil products led final energy consumption at 39.83% in 2024–25.
  • Thermal sources generated 77.01% of electricity in 2024–25, under the report's classification.
  • Installed capacity is measured in MW or GW; electricity generated is measured in kWh, MU or BU.
  • Trap: A fuel's share in electricity generation is not its share in total primary energy supply.

[Sources: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Energy Statistics India 2026, chapter 7, sections 7.1–7.4, and chapter 8, tables 8.11–8.13, printed pp. 113–114; released 30 March 2026, data for FY 2024–25 marked provisional; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Paired bars compare coal, crude oil and natural gas shares in India's primary energy supply, with a reminder that a smaller share need not mean less energy.
pictures.caption: Coal remained India's leading primary energy source between 2015–16 and 2024–25.

title: Understanding India's Energy Mix, Statistics and Trends

body:
Why different sectors consume different fuels

The choice of energy depends on the activity being performed. Road transport needs an energy carrier that can be stored on a vehicle, while heavy industry may require continuous high-temperature heat. A household commonly needs electricity for appliances and a convenient cooking fuel. Agriculture uses electricity or diesel for pumping and machinery.

SectorMajor energy usesImportant fuels or carriers
IndustryProcess heat, furnaces, machinery and feedstocksCoal, electricity, natural gas and petroleum products
TransportRoad, rail, air and water transportPetrol, diesel, aviation fuel, CNG and electricity
HouseholdsCooking, lighting, cooling and appliancesElectricity, LPG, PNG and biomass
AgricultureIrrigation pumps, tractors and machineryElectricity and diesel
FertilisersEnergy and chemical feedstockNatural gas, especially for ammonia production

In Energy Statistics India 2026, industry was the largest final-energy-consuming sector in 2024–25. Transport accounted for 23.68% of total final energy consumption. Within industrial energy consumption, iron and steel accounted for 22.42%. These percentages have different denominators: the first describes a share of all final energy, while the second describes a share within industry.

What import dependence means

Energy import dependence describes the extent to which a country's energy supply relies on imports from abroad. It is normally measured for a specified fuel, time period and accounting method.

India produces substantial quantities of coal but depends heavily on imported crude petroleum. It also imports natural gas, mainly as liquefied natural gas, and imports certain types of coal. Import dependence does not mean that domestic production is absent. It means domestic output does not fully meet the requirements represented by the selected energy-balance measure.

MoSPI's net energy import-dependency indicators for financial year 2024–25 were 89.44% for crude oil, 49.73% for natural gas and 23.50% for coal. These figures are provisional and were published on 30 March 2026.

For comparison, the indicators for 2015–16 were 84.59% for crude oil, 39.88% for natural gas and 27.34% for coal. Thus, crude-oil import dependence was substantially greater than coal import dependence in both periods. Natural-gas import dependence increased over the period, although its year-to-year movement was not uniform.

An import-dependency percentage must be interpreted using its source's definition. MoSPI's net energy-balance measure should not be presented as interchangeable with every crude-import percentage published using petroleum-product consumption or refinery throughput.

Why domestic coal does not eliminate coal imports

Coal differs in characteristics such as ash content, energy value and suitability for steel manufacture. India imports some coking coal required for metallurgical processes and also imports non-coking coal for certain power and industrial users. Import decisions depend on the required coal quality, availability, transport distance and costs. Domestic reserves therefore do not automatically remove the need for imported coal.

How import dependence creates vulnerability

Fuel imports expose India to changes in international prices, exchange rates, production decisions in exporting countries and interruptions to shipping or pipelines. If global crude-oil prices rise, the cost of importing crude can increase even when the number of barrels imported remains unchanged. Because international oil trade is commonly priced in US dollars, a weaker rupee can increase the rupee cost of imports.

A supply disruption can affect fuel availability; a price shock can affect affordability even when supplies continue. These are related but different aspects of energy security.

Dimensions of energy security

Energy security means maintaining sufficient, reliable and affordable energy supplies while managing environmental and strategic risks. Its major dimensions include:

  • Availability: obtaining enough domestic or imported fuel.
  • Affordability: keeping energy accessible to households, agriculture and industry.
  • Reliability: maintaining supplies during peak demand, equipment failures and external disruptions.
  • Diversity: avoiding excessive dependence on a single fuel, supplier, source region or transport route.
  • Sustainability: limiting pollution, greenhouse-gas emissions and long-term resource depletion.

Reducing oil consumption through efficient vehicles and electrification can reduce exposure to imported petroleum. However, if additional electricity comes mainly from coal, the change also affects coal demand and power-sector emissions. Energy-security policies must consider the entire chain rather than only the fuel used by the final consumer.

Prelims focus

  • Industry was India's largest final-energy-consuming sector in 2024–25 provisional data.
  • Transport accounted for 23.68% of total final energy consumption in that period.
  • MoSPI reported crude-oil import dependence of 89.44%, natural-gas dependence of 49.73% and coal dependence of 23.50% for 2024–25.
  • India imports coking coal as well as certain non-coking coal requirements.
  • Trap: Having domestic coal resources does not mean every industrially required coal grade is available in sufficient quantity.

[Sources: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Energy Statistics India 2026, chapter 7, section 7.3, and chapter 8, table 8.14 and figure 8.14, printed p. 115; released 30 March 2026, FY 2024–25 provisional; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 8, Infrastructure, section 8.5; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's import exposure differs greatly between crude oil, natural gas and coal.

title: Sectoral Energy Consumption, Import Dependence and Energy Security
